executive_summary: Enhanced geothermal is investable now at Series B and later stages. Fervo's public exit at $7.4 billion validates the technology and market, drilling costs have fallen by half in live deployments, and utilities are signing multi-year PPAs at utility scale. The main risks are permitting and interconnection delays, which cause schedule overruns averaging 59% even as drilling costs improve. Northbridge should source Series B+ deals in this window before late-stage pricing reflects the de-risking that has already occurred.

market_shifts.description: Fervo Energy achieved a 70% reduction in geothermal drilling time, with drilling costs across its first four horizontal wells at the Cape project falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million per well, demonstrating measurable cost reduction in EGS deployment.
In January 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act's investment and production tax credits were expanded to cover geothermal power, creating a new federal tax incentive structure for the sector.

In November 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy merged its geothermal office with its fossil energy office, creating a new Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy office, representing an organizational restructuring of federal support.
As of April 2025, 20 of the 24 wells required for what is expected to be the world's largest EGS development (500 MW capacity) had been completed, indicating progress toward utility-scale deployment.

Multiple LPs have asked Northbridge about exposure to 'firm, dispatchable clean power' as a category spanning both advanced nuclear and enhanced geothermal, framed as a hedge against intermittent renewables' grid integration challenges; the firm notes this cross-sub-segment 'dispatchability' framing from LPs is relatively new.

Inbound deal flow tagged 'enhanced geothermal' shows the average stage of inbound has shifted later (fewer seed-stage intros, more Series B+), which Northbridge reads as a possible sign the sub-segment is maturing past its earliest, most speculative phase.

incumbents.name: Fervo Energy
incumbents.differentiation: Achieved a 70% reduction in geothermal drilling time and demonstrated cost reduction from $9.4 million to $4.8 million per well across its first four horizontal wells; secured major utility-scale power purchase agreements including 31 MW with Shell Energy and 115 MW with Google; completed IPO on NASDAQ raising $1.89 billion at $7.39 billion valuation.

new_entrants.name: Eavor
new_entrants.differentiation: Uses a closed-loop geothermal energy design, distinguishing it from conventional open-loop or enhanced geothermal approaches.

new_entrants.name: Baseload
new_entrants.differentiation: Secured a 15-year power purchase agreement with Google for geothermal capacity, with deliveries to California's grid beginning in 2026.

new_entrants.name: Thermalis
new_entrants.differentiation: Uses directional drilling techniques adapted from oil & gas to make geothermal viable outside traditional volcanic/tectonic-boundary regions; Northbridge assessed the drilling technology itself as reasonably de-risked given its oil & gas heritage.

tensions_or_conflicts: Northbridge passed on Thermalis at Series B and noted the firm was NOT passing on EGS technology broadly, assessing the drilling approach as de-risked. External evidence since that decision shows Fervo cut drilling costs 49% well-to-well and completed a $7.4 billion IPO, suggesting the timing of Northbridge's pass may have been at the inflection point where technical de-risking was becoming visible in cost data and commercial traction.

Northbridge's internal tracking noted inbound deal flow shifting from seed to Series B+ as a sign of sector maturation. External funding data shows the opposite pattern: only $106 million raised across 3 rounds in Jan-Feb 2026, while Fervo raised $462 million in a single round in Dec 2025 and IPO'd five months later. This suggests capital is concentrating in one proven winner rather than distributing across a maturing cohort, which changes the sourcing strategy.

recommendations.text: Actively source Series B and Series C EGS developers using directional drilling adapted from oil and gas, targeting companies with signed utility PPAs or letters of intent. Fervo's cost curve (claim 9) and successful IPO (claim 2) demonstrate the technology works at scale, and utilities are signing multi-year contracts (claims 11, 12, 13). Northbridge already assessed this drilling approach as de-risked during Thermalis diligence (claim 19), and LPs are explicitly asking for exposure to firm dispatchable power (claim 21). The main risk is permitting and interconnection delays, which cause 59% average schedule overruns (claims 14, 16) and could push revenue timelines beyond what Series B/C cap tables can survive without bridge financing.

Run full diligence on the two earlier-stage EGS developers Northbridge tracked informally during the Thermalis review, if they have since raised Series B or signed utility PPAs. Claim 20 notes these companies pursue the same directional-drilling approach, and claim 22 shows inbound deal flow has shifted to later stages, meaning these companies may now be at a stage Northbridge would invest. The risk is that both companies remain pre-commercial or were acquired by Fervo or a utility, in which case this diligence yields no actionable deal but confirms the sector has consolidated faster than the quarterly scan suggested.

Monitor federal permitting reform and DOE geothermal funding deployment through Q4 2026, specifically tracking whether the $171.5 million field test funding (claim 5) flows to companies outside Fervo and whether the new Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy office (claim 6) accelerates lease auctions that claim 16 identifies as a bottleneck. The risk is that the DOE office merger signals deprioritization rather than acceleration, and that field test funding goes entirely to national labs or incumbents, in which case the monitoring reveals a narrowing opportunity rather than a broadening one.

Track whether Gridline Storage's customer conversations (claims 24, 25) about pairing storage with firm generation translate into a quantifiable procurement pattern among utilities, by asking two other energy portfolio companies to report similar signals in their next quarterly check-ins. If utilities are systematically modeling geothermal alongside storage rather than as competing solutions, that demand-side shift strengthens the case for prioritizing geothermal deals over additional storage investments. The risk is that this is customer speculation rather than budgeted procurement, in which case the two-quarter monitoring window clarifies intent without committing capital prematurely.

all_claims.claim: Fervo Energy raised a $462 million Series E round announced December 10, 2025, led by B Capital, with new investors including AllianceBernstein and Atacama.
The $462 million Series E brought Fervo Energy's total funding raised to date to $1.5 billion.
Fervo Energy completed an IPO on NASDAQ under ticker FRVO on May 13, 2026, raising $1.89 billion at an implied valuation of $7.39 billion.
Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) companies raised $106 million in equity funding across 3 rounds in the period from January through February 2026.
Eavor, a closed-loop geothermal energy company, raised $64.9 million in June 2025.
The U.S. Department of Energy announced a funding opportunity of up to $171.5 million for next-generation geothermal field tests, with Letters of Intent due in March.
In November 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy merged its geothermal office with its fossil energy office, creating a new Hydrocarbons and Geothermal Energy office.
In January 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act's investment and production tax credits were expanded to cover geothermal power.
As of April 2025, 20 of the 24 wells required for what is expected to be the world's largest EGS development (500 MW capacity) had been completed.
Fervo Energy reported a 70% reduction in geothermal drilling time, with drilling costs across the first four horizontal wells at its Cape project falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million per well.

A 2025 Stanford geothermal drilling cost curve update found that cost reduction for vertical wells ranges from 12% to 24%, while for horizontal wells the estimated cost reduction is between 18% and 26%.
Fervo Energy announced a 31 MW power purchase agreement with Shell Energy on April 15, 2025, with Shell Energy set to use the power for its retail load customers beginning in 2026.
Google signed a 115 MW power purchase agreement with Fervo Energy to provide firm, carbon-free electricity to the California grid, described as a major utility-scale contract for EGS.
A 15-year power purchase agreement between Google and Baseload was signed for geothermal capacity, with deliveries to California's grid beginning in 2026.

A study assessing construction project performance found geothermal projects averaged 58.8% schedule overruns, compared with 64% for nuclear builds, indicating geothermal projects still face significant timeline risk.
A Maryland state program to install geothermal energy systems in several housing complexes is facing delays amid concerns about cost effectiveness, as reported in July 2026.
Delays in EGS project development have been attributed to slow permitting and transmission interconnection processes, including a scarcity of geothermal lease auctions relative to demand.

An ITIF analysis published May 18, 2026 states a single EGS well costs between $5 million and $10 million to drill, noting per-well costs have improved from a range as high as $13 million down toward $5 million as drilling rates have improved.

Northbridge ran diligence on an enhanced geothermal systems developer (internal codename 'Thermalis') during its Series B raise; Thermalis uses directional drilling techniques adapted from oil & gas to make geothermal viable outside traditional volcanic/tectonic-boundary regions.

Northbridge passed on the Thermalis deal, but explicitly did NOT pass due to technical skepticism about EGS as an approach; the firm's technical advisor assessed the drilling technology itself as reasonably de-risked given its oil & gas heritage, and the memo notes the pass was thesis-specific to this one company, not a signal against enhanced geothermal broadly.

During the same Thermalis review cycle, Northbridge informally tracked two other earlier-stage (seed/Series A) EGS developers pursuing a similar directional-drilling approach, suggesting this may be converging as the dominant technical approach in the sub-segment rather than one company's differentiated bet; the firm did not run full diligence on either.

Multiple LPs have asked Northbridge about its exposure (or lack thereof) to 'firm, dispatchable clean power' as a category spanning both advanced nuclear and enhanced geothermal, framed as a hedge against intermittent renewables' grid integration challenges; the firm notes this cross-sub-segment 'dispatchability' framing from LPs is relatively new.

Inbound deal flow tagged 'enhanced geothermal' was roughly flat quarter-over-quarter as of the most recent quarterly scan, but the average stage of inbound has shifted later (fewer seed-stage intros, more Series B+), which the firm reads as a possible sign the sub-segment is maturing past its earliest, most speculative phase.

The quarterly sector scan is explicitly caveated as directional and unverified, drawing on inbound deal flow, LP conversations, and informal market chatter rather than formal diligence, and is meant to flag patterns before any single sub-segment gets a formal diligence memo.

In a routine check-in with portfolio company Gridline Storage Systems (a grid-scale battery storage company, not itself a geothermal company), Gridline's CEO reported that utility customers in two recent customer conversations specifically named advanced nuclear or geothermal as an assumed firm-generation source to be modeled alongside storage, rather than treating storage as a standalone intermittency solution.

Northbridge treats this Gridline customer signal as a useful but non-systematic demand-side data point suggesting a 'storage plus firm generation' procurement pattern among utilities, which could be a tailwind for geothermal and advanced nuclear that doesn't show up in either sub-segment's own deal-flow data directly; the firm explicitly cautions this is one portfolio company's customer conversations, not a quantified market survey.
